source: Due South Outfitters + Fly Life Outdoors

conditions.overall: High Country streams in Watauga, Ashe, and Avery Counties are running at seasonal early-summer levels. Conditions are generally favorable for dry fly and nymph fishing across the region.

top_flies.name: Yellow Sally Stonefly
top_flies.note: Prime early summer pattern for high-elevation NC streams; fish during midday hatches along riffles and pocket water.

top_flies.name: Sulphur Comparadun
top_flies.note: Effective during evening sulphur hatches; drift drag-free in slower runs and tailouts.

top_flies.name: Elk Hair Caddis
top_flies.note: Reliable searching dry fly for pocket water and riffles throughout the day.

top_flies.name: Pheasant Tail Nymph
top_flies.note: Versatile subsurface pattern; dead-drift near the bottom in runs and pools.

top_flies.name: Hare's Ear Nymph
top_flies.note: Good all-around nymph; fish under an indicator in moderate-depth pools and runs.

top_flies.name: Zebra Midge
top_flies.note: Productive in slower pools and tailwaters, especially during lower-light periods.

top_flies.name: Stimulator
top_flies.note: Use as a dry-dropper anchor in faster pocket water and around plunge pools.

tactics: Focus fishing effort during cooler morning and evening windows when trout are most active at high-elevation streams.
Use a dry-dropper rig with a larger attractor dry (Stimulator or Elk Hair Caddis) and a small nymph dropper to cover both surface and subsurface feeding lanes simultaneously.
High Country streams near Boone run 1-2 weeks behind lower-elevation WNC streams — adjust hatch timing expectations accordingly.
Approach runs and pools with a low profile and longer leaders (9-12 ft) as water clarity is high and fish can be spooky.
Target shaded pocket water and undercut banks during midday when temperatures peak, as trout seek thermal refuge.
During sulphur and Yellow Sally hatches, match size and silhouette precisely and present with a drag-free drift using reach or curve casts.
Nymph deep along the bottom of slower pools and runs where larger fish hold during low-pressure midday hours.

waters.name: New River (South Fork)
waters.note: Ashe County's signature water; running clear and fishable — focus on slower flats and seams with sulphur patterns in the evening.

waters.name: North Fork New River
waters.note: Good early-summer conditions; target pocket water with dry-dropper rigs and small nymphs.

waters.name: Watauga River
waters.note: Main stem flowing through Watauga County; clear conditions favor precise presentations and longer leaders for wary fish.

waters.name: Elk Creek
waters.note: Watauga County tributary; classic freestone stream — fish riffles and plunge pools with Yellow Sallies and Elk Hair Caddis.

waters.name: Linville River
waters.note: Avery County — high-gradient stream running cool and clear; excellent pocket water fishing with attractor dries.

waters.name: Cranberry Creek
waters.note: Avery County tributary; smaller stream requiring stealthy approach — ideal for tight-loop casts in canopied sections.

waters.name: Beaver Creek
waters.note: Ashe County; productive for wild trout — fish early morning before recreational pressure increases.

elevation_note: High Country streams near Boone (3,300-4,000 ft) run 1-2 weeks behind lower-elevation WNC — hatches and seasonal patterns arrive later than reports from lower-elevation waters suggest.
